relevance_reason: Only the abstract was available. It describes a consensus expert reclassification of inherited epidermolysis bullosa and related skin fragility disorders. It does not mention junctional EB 5A or the intermediate subtype specifically, so it only gives nomenclature context.

findings.statement: Has et al. (2020) reported an international expert consensus reclassification of inherited epidermolysis bullosa (EB), which updated the 2014 classification using new clinical and molecular data. The authors introduced the concept of genetic disorders with skin fragility, with classical EB as the prototype. They classified other skin fragility disorders, such as peeling skin, erosive, hyperkeratotic and connective tissue disorders, as separate 'EB-related' categories.
quotes: We sought to reclassify disorders with skin fragility, with a focus on EB, based on new clinical and molecular data.
we introduce the concept of genetic disorders with skin fragility, of which classical EB represents the prototype.
These include peeling skin disorders, erosive disorders, hyperkeratotic disorders, and connective tissue disorders with skin fragility.

relevance_reason: Reports a patient with a mild, non-lethal ITGB4-related epidermolysis bullosa (no pyloric atresia) caused by an ITGB4 mutation. This is the ITGB4 non-Herlitz/intermediate phenotype.

findings.statement: Jonkman et al. (2002) reported a 49-year-old woman who had mild blistering of the hands and feet from birth, nail dystrophy with onychogryposis, and enamel hypoplasia. She had no alopecia and no history of pyloric atresia. Electron microscopy and antigen mapping of a skin blister showed that the split was intraepidermal, low in the basal keratinocytes through the attachment plaque of the hemidesmosome. The authors described the phenotype as having predominant features of epidermolysis bullosa simplex.
quotes: The patient, a 49-y-old female, had mild blistering of hands and feet from birth on, dystrophy of the nails with onychogryposis, and enamel hypoplasia. She had no alopecia and no history of pyloric atresia.
Electron microscopy and antigen mapping of a skin blister revealed that the level of separation was intraepidermal, low in the basal keratinocytes through the attachment plaque of the hemidesmosome.

phenotypes.text: mild blistering of hands and feet
intraepidermal blister cleavage within basal keratinocytes

findings.statement: In the patient, Jonkman et al. (2002) found a novel heterozygous 2-bp deletion (4733delCT) in the ITGB4 gene. The deletion caused in-frame skipping of exon 36, which was predicted to remove 50 amino acids (residues 1450-1499) within the third fibronectin type III repeat of the beta-4 cytoplasmic domain. Immunoblot analysis showed a beta-4 polypeptide 5 kDa shorter than normal. Because no full-size protein was detected in vitro and the 450-11A epitope was absent in vivo, the authors expected the patient to also be heterozygous for a null allele.
quotes: At the molecular level the phenotype was caused by a novel 2 bp deletion 4733delCT in ITGB4, resulting in in-frame skipping of exon 36 and a deduced 50 amino acid deletion (1450-1499) within the third fibronectin type III repeat

The 4733delCT mutation was heterozygously present in the DNA. The patient is also expected to be heterozygous for a null allele, as no full-size protein was detected in vitro and the epitope 450-11 A was absent in vivo.

findings.statement: Jonkman et al. (2002) used immunofluorescence microscopy of the patient's skin. Monoclonal antibody 450-11A, which recognizes the third fibronectin III repeat in the intracellular domain of integrin beta-4, did not bind at all. Binding of monoclonal antibodies against epitopes at the amino- and carboxy-terminal ends of the protein was reduced.
quotes: Immuno-fluorescence microscopy revealed absent binding of monoclonal antibody 450-11 A against the third fibronectin III repeat on the intracellular domain of integrin beta4, whereas binding was reduced with monoclonal antibodies recognizing epitopes on amino-terminal and carboxy-terminal ends of the polypeptide.

findings.statement: Jonkman et al. (2002) concluded that deleting the third fibronectin type III repeat in the integrin beta-4 cytoplasmic domain is clinically pathogenic. This repeat is thought to interact with BP180/type XVII collagen. They concluded that its loss results in a mild phenotype with predominant features of epidermolysis bullosa simplex.
quotes: These data show that deletion of the third fibronectin type III repeat in the cytoplasmic domain of integrin beta4, which is thought to interact with BP180/type XVII collagen, is clinically pathogenic and results in a mild phenotype with predominant features of epidermolysis bullosa simplex.

relevance_reason: The title reports a homozygous ITGB4 missense mutation (G931D) that causes non-Herlitz junctional epidermolysis bullosa without pyloric atresia, which is the subject of this entry.

findings.statement: Inoue et al. (2000) identified a homozygous missense mutation, G931D, in the cytoplasmic tail of beta-4 integrin in non-Herlitz junctional epidermolysis bullosa without pyloric atresia. They reported that the mutation disrupted hemidesmosome assembly.
quotes: A homozygous missense mutation in the cytoplasmic tail of beta4 integrin, G931D, that disrupts hemidesmosome assembly and underlies Non-Herlitz junctional epidermolysis bullosa without pyloric atresia?

relevance_reason: The paper describes two patients with mild, surviving pyloric atresia-junctional EB who carried compound heterozygous ITGB4 mutations. This fits the intermediate/non-Herlitz JEB5A phenotype.

findings.statement: Mellerio et al. (1998) reported 2 unrelated patients with junctional epidermolysis bullosa with pyloric atresia who survived into early childhood and had mild skin involvement. This differed from the usual course of the disorder, which is often fatal within the first weeks or months of life even after surgical correction.
quotes: We report two unrelated patients with this disease who have survived into early childhood with mild cutaneous involvement
This disease is usually fatal within the first few weeks or months of life even following surgical correction of the intestinal obstruction.

findings.statement: In a patient with mild pyloric atresia-junctional epidermolysis bullosa, Mellerio et al. (1998) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the ITGB4 gene: a splice site mutation in exon 30 (3793+1G-A) and a nonsense mutation in exon 36 (W1478X). The authors suggested that the nonsense mutation would markedly reduce beta-4 integrin mRNA, but that the splice site allele might still allow some functional, though altered, beta-4 polypeptide to be made.
quotes: The first patient was a compound heterozygote for a splice site mutation in exon 30 (3793 + 1G-to-A) and a non-sense mutation in exon 36 (W1478X)
the presence of the missense or splice site mutation on the second allele may enable the synthesis of some functional, albeit perturbed, beta4 polypeptide

findings.statement: In a second, unrelated patient with mild pyloric atresia-junctional epidermolysis bullosa, Mellerio et al. (1998) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the ITGB4 gene: a missense mutation in exon 3 (C38R) and a 1-bp deletion in exon 36 (4776delG). The authors suggested that the missense allele might allow some functional beta-4 integrin to be synthesized, which could explain the mild phenotype.
quotes: the second was a compound heterozygote for a missense mutation in exon 3 (C38R) and a 1 bp deletion in exon 36 (4776delG)
Although the non-sense and deletion mutations are predicted to result in markedly reduced beta4 integrin mRNA levels

relevance_reason: The paper describes ITGB4 mutations in the lethal form of epidermolysis bullosa with pyloric atresia, not the nonlethal intermediate JEB5A phenotype. It gives allelic and gene-level context only.

findings.statement: In 3 patients with the lethal form of epidermolysis bullosa with pyloric atresia (EB-PA), Pulkkinen et al. (1998) identified novel ITGB4 mutations on 5 alleles. They screened each ITGB4 exon by PCR, heteroduplex analysis and direct sequencing. One patient was homozygous for a 2-bp deletion in exon 34 (4501delTC).
quotes: we have explored the molecular pathology of the lethal form of EB-PA, and we describe novel ITGB4 mutations in five alleles of three patients
The novel mutations included a homozygous 2-bp deletion in exon 34 (4501delTC)

findings.statement: Pulkkinen et al. (1998) found that a patient with lethal EB-PA was compound heterozygous for two ITGB4 mutations. The paternal allele carried a 2-bp deletion in exon 3 (120delTG). The maternal allele carried a cysteine substitution in exon 7 (C245G) in the extracellular domain, which the authors suggested may affect ligand binding or alpha6-beta4 dimerization.
quotes: compound heterozygosity for a 2-bp deletion within the paternal allele (120delTG) within exon 3 and a cysteine substitution in the maternal allele (C245G) within exon 7
the missense mutation in the extracellular domain of beta4 integrin may affect ligand binding or dimerization of alpha6 and beta4 integrin subunits

findings.statement: In a third patient with lethal EB-PA, Pulkkinen et al. (1998) identified a paternal nonsense mutation in exon 4 of ITGB4 (Q73X). Three of the four distinct mutations were predicted to produce truncated polypeptides.
quotes: and the paternal nonsense mutation within exon 4 (Q73X)
three of four distinct mutations predicted truncated polypeptide chains

findings.statement: Pulkkinen et al. (1998) noted that EB-PA is a clinically and genetically heterogeneous autosomal recessive blistering disorder that includes lethal and nonlethal variants.
quotes: Epidermolysis bullosa with pyloric atresia (EB-PA; OMIM 226730) is a clinically and genetically heterogeneous autosomal recessive blistering disorder, including lethal and nonlethal variants.
